itens.t: Trump expects to meet with Xi and Putin at upcoming summit
itens.r: U.S. President Donald Trump announced on Sunday that he expects to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin during an upcoming international summit next week. The diplomatic meetings come as global leaders gather to address major geopolitical and economic issues. White House officials are finalizing the schedules for the separate bilateral discussions. The anticipated encounters mark a significant moment in ongoing international relations among the major powers.
itens.d:
US President Donald Trump stated that he expects to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin during an APEC summit in China. The gathering is scheduled for November 18 and 19 in Shenzhen, where discussions will cover multiple issues, including denuclearization and ending the war in Iran.

In October, Trump expressed openness to trilateral arms control talks. Meanwhile, Putin previously suggested utilizing such a meeting to address the prolonged conflict in Ukraine. In an interview with CBS, Trump also noted that he believes they are very close to reaching an agreement to end the Russia-Ukraine war.
itens.e:
US President Donald Trump stated that he expects to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin during an upcoming APEC summit scheduled for November 18 and 19 in Shenzhen. Discussions at the gathering are expected to cover multiple issues, including denuclearization and ending the war in Iran. In October, Trump expressed openness to trilateral arms control talks, while Putin previously suggested utilizing such a meeting to address the prolonged conflict in Ukraine.

This high-level diplomatic engagement directly involves global superpowers and carries significant implications for international security and ongoing conflicts. In an interview with CBS, Trump noted that he believes they are very close to reaching an agreement to end the Russia-Ukraine war, making the prospective trilateral discussions a critical venue for potential geopolitical shifts.

One risk is whether these anticipated talks will yield concrete diplomatic breakthroughs on complex issues like arms control and regional wars. Observers should watch for further confirmation of the summit's agenda and any preliminary bilateral or trilateral coordination leading up to the November gathering in Shenzhen.

itens.t: Seoul stocks close lower amid uncertainties in the artificial intelligence sector
itens.r: Seoul stocks closed lower on Monday as investors digested mounting uncertainties in the artificial intelligence sector. Market sentiment was dampened by developments including an internal probe at Nvidia Corp.
itens.d:
Seoul stocks closed lower as investors digested uncertainties facing the artificial intelligence sector, including an internal probe at Nvidia Corp. following allegations its chief was targeted by a Chinese spy. The local currency strengthened against the US dollar.

After rocky trading, the benchmark Korea Composite Stock Price Index dropped 40.84 points to finish at 5,018.85. Trade volume remained light at 231.8 million shares worth 17.26 trillion won.
itens.e:
Seoul stocks closed lower as investors digested ongoing uncertainties facing the artificial intelligence sector. Market sentiment was weighed down by developments including an internal probe at Nvidia Corp. following allegations its chief was targeted by a Chinese spy. Amid this rocky trading environment, the benchmark Korea Composite Stock Price Index dropped 40.84 points to finish at 5,018.85, accompanied by light trade volume of 231.8 million shares worth 17.26 trillion won.

This market downturn directly affects domestic investors and reflects how global technology sector vulnerabilities can swiftly transmit to regional financial exchanges. While local equities faced downward pressure, the local currency conversely strengthened against the US dollar, illustrating a divergent response across different segments of the domestic financial landscape.

One risk is that persistent anxieties surrounding artificial intelligence and corporate governance probes could continue to trigger volatility in Asian markets. Investors will need to watch whether technology bellwethers like Nvidia resolve their internal investigations and how broader sectoral confidence stabilizes in upcoming trading sessions.

itens.t: Special counsel bill deepens partisan rift over impact on Lee's suspended trials
itens.r: A new special counsel bill targeting investigations from the previous administration has sparked intense partisan debate in South Korea. Lawmakers remain deeply divided over how the legislation might affect ongoing legal proceedings.
itens.d:
A special counsel bill aimed at uncovering politically motivated investigations under former President Yoon Suk Yeol is deepening a partisan divide over its impact on criminal cases against President Lee Jae Myung. The ruling bloc argues the probe is necessary because Lee and other liberal leaders were unfairly indicted with fabricated evidence, while conservative opposition parties call for his impeachment and accuse Lee of abusing power.

The dispute intensified as Justice Minister nominee Lee Yong-cheol stated he would handle calls to drop charges against Lee in accordance with the law and principles. This marked a different stance from his predecessor, prompting the main opposition party to question his nomination.

itens.t: South Korea deploys mine-hunting assets to anti-piracy unit near Strait of Hormuz
itens.r: Defense Minister Kang Shin-chul announced that South Korea is deploying mine-hunting assets to its anti-piracy naval unit. The move is designed to prepare for unseen security threats in the vital waterway.
itens.d:
Defense Minister Kang Shin-chul stated that South Korea's decision to expand its anti-piracy naval unit's operational scope with mine-hunting assets aims to prepare for potential threats near the Strait of Hormuz that cannot be entirely ruled out. Seoul plans to extend the Cheonghae Unit's reach to south of Oman in the Arabian Sea.

Authorities are also seeking to deploy mine-sweeping equipment, an explosive ordnance disposal team, and a maritime patrol aircraft. Although officials stressed the move protects commercial ships from piracy, critics argue it serves as a de facto military contribution to the U.S. conflict with Iran.

itens.t: Prison terms sought for ex-security officials over THAAD intelligence leak
itens.r: South Korean prosecutors have demanded prison sentences for three former security officials under the previous administration. The defendants are accused of leaking classified intelligence related to the U.S. THAAD missile defense system.
itens.d:
The prosecution sought prison terms for three former officials under President Moon Jae-in over allegations of leaking intelligence related to the THAAD U.S. missile defense system. Prosecutors requested 10-month prison sentences for former national security adviser Chung Eui-yong and former defense minister Jeong Kyeong-doo.

A two-year prison term was requested for former first deputy national security adviser Suh Choo-suk. The officials are accused of ordering or instructing staff to inform activists in advance about operations to replace THAAD battery equipment and materials in Seongju.

itens.t: Fifty-ninth anniversary of the Saturn V rocket launch amid a new space race
itens.r: The historic first flight of the Saturn V rocket occurred 59 years ago, marking a monumental milestone in aerospace history. Standing 110 meters tall, the powerful rocket was essential for the uncrewed Apollo 4 mission to test critical space exploration technology.
itens.d:
Fifty-nine years ago, the first flight of the Saturn V rocket launched to test NASA technology designed to take humans to the Moon and bring them back safely. The 110-meter rocket used three stages, which were discarded as they consumed fuel to reduce weight and facilitate its ascent.

To simulate a return journey from the Moon, NASA accelerated the spacecraft to roughly 40,000 kilometers per hour before reentering the atmosphere. The historic testing paved the way for humanity to reach the lunar surface just two years later with Apollo 11.

itens.t: Scientists simulate an abiotic Earth to aid the search for alien life
itens.r: Researchers have developed a novel computer simulation depicting a rocky planet without life to help astronomers identify true biosignatures. This technological tool aims to improve the search for habitable worlds and extraterrestrial life across the universe.
itens.d:
A new computer simulation depicting a rocky planet without life has been developed to aid scientists in the quest to discover alien life. Distinguishing inhabited planets from habitable ones can be difficult because some atmospheric gases are produced by both biology and geology.

Created by Samantha Gilbert-Janizek, the model simulates 19 non-life-related properties of a rocky planet, including stellar heat and subsurface gas outflows. The tool helps researchers understand how habitable but non-living planets might mimic living ones.

itens.t: NASA confirms the annual Antarctic ozone hole reaches its maximum extent for 2026
itens.r: NASA and NOAA observations indicate that the seasonal Antarctic ozone hole has reached its peak area for 2026. Monitoring data continues to provide crucial insights into the long-term recovery of Earth's stratospheric ozone layer.
itens.d:
A data visualization highlights the area and shape of the annual Antarctic ozone hole on its maximum extent day. Scientists define the ozone hole as the region where ozone concentrations drop below the historical threshold of 220 Dobson units.

The stratospheric ozone layer protects life on Earth by absorbing ultraviolet light that damages DNA and causes skin cancer. British researchers first reported dramatic thinning over Antarctica in 1985, leading to widespread satellite monitoring of the phenomenon.

itens.t: Germany's Henkel to open advanced R&D center for AI chip materials in Seoul
itens.r: German industrial materials maker Henkel is establishing a new research and development center in Seoul. The facility will focus on creating specialized packaging materials for high-bandwidth memory and artificial intelligence chips.
itens.d:
German adhesives and materials maker Henkel will establish a research center in Seoul to develop packaging materials for artificial intelligence chips and high-bandwidth memory. The Seoul Metropolitan Government signed a memorandum of understanding with the company for the project.

Henkel will invest 12.1 billion won and hire 15 new researchers for the facility, located in the Gasan Digital Complex. The center will combine existing research operations with new development focused on advanced semiconductor packaging materials.
